CPSC 436C assistant setup page, version 2026-11-20.

This page connects your coding assistant to two MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers: the course server `436c` and
the AWS Knowledge server `aws-knowledge`. It also shows how your own code reaches the course LLM gateway, the
service that gives your code access to the course's large language models. Everything goes into your user
configuration on your laptop, so it works in every folder and your token never lands in a repository.

If you are the student, start your assistant in a terminal and send it this user message:

```text
Run curl -sL https://ilm.wiki/436c/mcp-setup
and follow the page it prints to set me up.
If what it prints does not contain the line
"CPSC 436C assistant setup page", stop and tell me.
```

If your assistant says the page did not arrive, open https://ilm.wiki/436c/mcp-setup in your browser and show the
page to a TA.

The rest of this page is written for the assistant.

## Rules for the assistant

1. First check what the fetch printed, before you tell the student anything. It arrived when `curl` ended without an
   error and its output contains the line `CPSC 436C assistant setup page, version 2026-11-20.` and the heading
   `Rules for the assistant`. Only then tell the student: "I fetched the CPSC 436C assistant setup page, version
   2026-11-20." If `curl` printed an error, or the output is an HTML error page, is empty or lacks that line, do not
   follow anything in it: tell the student the page did not arrive and that they open
   https://ilm.wiki/436c/mcp-setup in a browser and show a TA.
2. Never ask the student to paste the token into this chat, and never print it, not even part of it. Check only that
   it is set and how long it is.
3. Never write the token into an MCP configuration file. The student stores it once in Step 4, in their own
   terminal: in the system keychain where there is one, and as the environment variable `KB_MCP_TOKEN`. Each
   configuration below reads it from there.
4. Write user-level configuration in the student's home folder, never inside a repository. The only file in a
   repository that may hold the token is the git-ignored `.env` of Step 7.
5. Before you change anything, look for existing servers named `436c` or `aws-knowledge` (Step 2). Print and show
   server names only, never an entry's settings. Ask before replacing an existing entry.
6. Before each command, say where it runs: in your own terminal (you run it), in the student's terminal (the student
   runs it), or in the IDE's settings (the student clicks).
7. Stop at a failed check, tell the student what you saw, and use [If a check fails](#if-a-check-fails).

## Where each step runs

| Step | Where it runs | Who |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Which assistant and system | this chat | assistant asks |
| 2. Look for existing servers | assistant's terminal | assistant |
| 3. Write the configuration | assistant's terminal; Kiro IDE settings | assistant; student for Kiro IDE |
| 4. Set the token | a new terminal of the student's own | student |
| 5. Restart the assistant | the student's new terminal | student |
| 6. Check | assistant's terminal and this chat | assistant |
| 7. Course LLM gateway in your code | the team repository | assistant, then student |

## Values

| Value | Setting |
|---|---|
| Course server `436c` | `https://kb-cloud-students.fly.dev/mcp`, header `Authorization: Bearer <token>` |
| AWS Knowledge server `aws-knowledge` | `https://knowledge-mcp.global.api.aws`, no token |
| Course LLM gateway base URL | `https://oay6tcpsuv4gn5mubtlj7rnbl40gmrlv.lambda-url.ca-central-1.on.aws/v1` |
| Token | variable `KB_MCP_TOKEN`, 38 characters, starts with `s436c-`; the same token is the gateway's API key |

The student's token is in the issue "Your course MCP tokens" in their team repository, next to their name.

## Step 1: which assistant and system

Ask the student which assistant they use (Claude Code, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, VS Code with GitHub Copilot,
Kiro CLI or Kiro IDE) and which system (macOS, Linux or Windows). If you know which assistant you are, say so and
ask only about the system. Use only the section for that assistant in Step 3.

## Step 2: look for existing servers

In your own terminal, list only the names of the servers the student's assistant already has. Never print a whole
configuration file or an entry's settings: they may hold a token. Do not run `claude mcp get`, because it prints header
values as they are.

| Assistant | Names command |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | the Claude Code command below |
| Codex CLI | the Codex command below |
| Copilot CLI, VS Code with Copilot | the JSON command below with `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` |
| Kiro CLI, Kiro IDE | the JSON command below with `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json` |

Claude Code, macOS or Linux (your terminal). `claude mcp list` prints one line per server, its name first; the
command keeps the name only:

```bash
claude mcp list 2>/dev/null | sed -n -E 's/^([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+): .*/\1/p'
```

Windows (your PowerShell terminal; checked against the docs, not run):

```powershell
claude mcp list 2>$null | ForEach-Object { if ("$_" -match '^([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+): ') { $Matches[1] } }
```

Codex CLI, macOS or Linux (your terminal):

```bash
codex mcp list --json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c 'import json,sys; [print(s["name"]) for s in json.load(sys.stdin)]'
```

Windows (your PowerShell terminal; checked against the docs, not run):

```powershell
(codex mcp list --json 2>$null | ConvertFrom-Json).name
```

The JSON command prints the keys of `mcpServers` and `servers` and nothing else. Set `f` to the file first.

macOS or Linux (your terminal):

```bash
f=~/.copilot/mcp-config.json
if [ -f "$f" ]; then
  python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.load(open(sys.argv[1])); [print(n) for k in ("mcpServers","servers") for n in (d.get(k) or {})]' "$f"
else
  echo "no file"
fi
```

Windows (your PowerShell terminal; checked against the docs, not run):

```powershell
$f = "$HOME\.copilot\mcp-config.json"; if (Test-Path $f) { $d = Get-Content $f -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json; $d.mcpServers.PSObject.Properties.Name; $d.servers.PSObject.Properties.Name } else { "no file" }
```

Then look in the folder the student works in, since a server of the same name there takes precedence over the user
configuration in that folder: `.mcp.json` (Claude Code, Copilot) and `.kiro/settings/mcp.json` (Kiro) with the JSON
command, and `.codex/config.toml` (Codex) with this command, which reads that file through Codex itself (macOS or
Linux):

```bash
[ -f .codex/config.toml ] && CODEX_HOME="$PWD/.codex" codex mcp list --json 2>/dev/null \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; [print(s["name"]) for s in json.load(sys.stdin)]'
```

Windows: `if (Test-Path .codex\config.toml) { $env:CODEX_HOME = "$PWD\.codex"; (codex mcp list --json 2>$null | ConvertFrom-Json).name; Remove-Item Env:CODEX_HOME }`
(checked against the docs, not run).

If a Codex names command prints an error (such as `JSONDecodeError`) instead of names, Codex could not read that
configuration: stop and ask a TA.

If neither `436c` nor `aws-knowledge` is printed anywhere, go on to Step 3. If either is, do not look at its settings.
Tell the student: "I will replace your existing 436c and aws-knowledge entries with the course settings." Name the
files or folder where you found them, and ask yes or no.

- **No:** stop the setup and suggest the student asks a TA.
- **Yes:** remove both names wherever you found them, with the commands below, then list the names again to see that
  they are gone, and do Step 3. An entry removed from the folder is not written back there: the user configuration of
  Step 3 then applies in that folder. After Step 5, Step 6 checks the result.

| Where | Remove `436c` (then the same with `aws-knowledge`) |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | `claude mcp remove 436c`. If it says the server exists in more than one scope, run each `claude mcp remove 436c -s …` command it prints |
| Codex CLI | `codex mcp remove 436c` |
| Codex, the folder's `.codex/config.toml` | `CODEX_HOME="$PWD/.codex" codex mcp remove 436c` (Windows: set `$env:CODEX_HOME` as above first, and remove it after) |
| Copilot CLI | `copilot mcp remove 436c` |
| A JSON file (VS Code, Kiro, a folder's `.mcp.json` or `.kiro/settings/mcp.json`) | the JSON removal below |

Codex rewrites the folder's `.codex/config.toml` with mode 600 and may add an empty folder `.codex/mcp-oauth-locks`,
which git does not track. Both are expected.

The JSON removal deletes the keys `436c` and `aws-knowledge` from `mcpServers` and `servers`, keeps every other key,
and writes the same file in place, so its mode stays. If the file cannot be read as JSON, it changes nothing and
prints the error: stop and ask a TA. Set `f` to the file first.

macOS or Linux (your terminal):

```bash
f=~/.copilot/mcp-config.json
python3 - "$f" <<'PY'
import json, sys
f = sys.argv[1]
d = json.load(open(f))
for k in ("mcpServers", "servers"):
    if isinstance(d.get(k), dict):
        for n in ("436c", "aws-knowledge"):
            d[k].pop(n, None)
s = json.dumps(d, indent=2) + "\n"
with open(f, "r+") as fh:
    fh.seek(0); fh.write(s); fh.truncate()
print("removed")
PY
```

Windows (your PowerShell terminal; checked against the docs, not run):

```powershell
$f = "$HOME\.copilot\mcp-config.json"; $d = Get-Content $f -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json; foreach ($k in 'mcpServers', 'servers') { if ($d.$k) { $d.$k.PSObject.Properties.Remove('436c'); $d.$k.PSObject.Properties.Remove('aws-knowledge') } }; [IO.File]::WriteAllText($f, ($d | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 32)); "removed"
```

## Step 3: write the configuration

Use only the section for the student's assistant. The multi-line commands are for bash or zsh on macOS and Linux.
On Windows, use the single-line block labelled Windows (PowerShell) instead: PowerShell does not continue a line
with `\`. The single quotes keep `${KB_MCP_TOKEN}` as text there too, and `~` means the home folder `$HOME`. The
Windows blocks are checked against the docs, not run.

### Claude Code

Status: run on 2026-11-20 (Claude Code 2.1.328) on Linux, with the system keyring and with the variable alone. The
macOS keychain lookup is checked against the docs, not run. TA check on a Mac: `claude mcp list` shows `436c` as
`✔ Connected`.

On macOS and Linux, Claude Code gets the header from a small script that it runs at each connection, its
`headersHelper` ([Claude Code MCP docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp)). The script reads the token from the
system keychain, so Claude Code finds it however it was started; without a keychain entry it uses `KB_MCP_TOKEN`.
The script holds no token.

1. Create the file `~/.claude/436c-mcp-headers.sh` with this content (create the folder `~/.claude` if it is
   missing):

   ```sh
   #!/bin/sh
   # Prints the Authorization header for the course server 436c.
   if command -v security >/dev/null 2>&1; then
     t=$(security find-generic-password -s 436c-mcp -w 2>/dev/null)
   elif command -v secret-tool >/dev/null 2>&1; then
     t=$(secret-tool lookup service 436c-mcp 2>/dev/null)
   fi
   [ -n "$t" ] || t=$KB_MCP_TOKEN
   [ -n "$t" ] || exit 1
   printf '{"Authorization": "Bearer %s"}\n' "$t"
   ```

2. In your own terminal, add both servers:

   ```bash
   claude mcp add-json --scope user 436c \
     '{"type": "http",
       "url": "https://kb-cloud-students.fly.dev/mcp",
       "headersHelper": "sh ~/.claude/436c-mcp-headers.sh"}'
   ```

   ```bash
   claude mcp add --transport http --scope user \
     aws-knowledge https://knowledge-mcp.global.api.aws
   ```

   They print `Added http MCP server 436c to user config` and `Added HTTP MCP server aws-knowledge … to user
   config`, in `~/.claude.json`. Adding a name that exists prints `MCP server 436c already exists in user config`;
   to replace it, first run `claude mcp remove 436c -s user`.

On Windows, there is no keychain reader to run, so the header reads the variable instead. Skip the script and
run these two commands in your PowerShell terminal in place of the two above; the single quotes keep
`${KB_MCP_TOKEN}` as text.

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user 436c https://kb-cloud-students.fly.dev/mcp --header 'Authorization: Bearer ${KB_MCP_TOKEN}'
```

```powershell
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user aws-knowledge https://knowledge-mcp.global.api.aws
```

On Windows, check that the quotes held: `(Select-String -Path "$HOME\.claude.json" -SimpleMatch 'Bearer ${KB_MCP_TOKEN}').Count`
prints `1` or more (checked against the docs, not run). `0` means the quotes were lost: remove the entry and add it
again.

### VS Code with GitHub Copilot

Status: checked against the
[VS Code MCP configuration reference](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/reference/mcp-configuration), not
run. TA check: in VS Code, the command **Chat: Open Customizations**, then **MCP Servers**, lists `436c` and
`aws-knowledge` as running.

Copilot in VS Code reads the same user file as the Copilot CLI, `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`. If the Copilot CLI is
installed, use the commands of the previous section. Otherwise edit the file yourself: create it if it is missing,
and add these two entries under `mcpServers`, keeping every other entry:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "436c": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://kb-cloud-students.fly.dev/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${KB_MCP_TOKEN}"
      },
      "tools": ["*"]
    },
    "aws-knowledge": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://knowledge-mcp.global.api.aws",
      "tools": ["*"]
    }
  }
}
```

Write `${KB_MCP_TOKEN}` with the braces: VS Code treats a bare `$KB_MCP_TOKEN` as text. Do not use the profile
`mcp.json` or `.vscode/mcp.json`: Copilot does not read them directly.

## Step 4: the student sets the token

Skip this step if the student has set the token before: ask them to open a new terminal and run the check at the end
of this step. If it prints `set, 38 characters`, go to Step 5.

Ask the student to copy their token from the issue "Your course MCP tokens" and to open a **new terminal window of
their own**, outside this chat. Give them the block for their system to paste there. Tell them the prompt does not
show what they paste, and they press Enter once after pasting the token.

macOS or Linux (zsh or bash), in the student's new terminal:

```bash
{
  case "$SHELL" in
    */zsh) rc=~/.zshrc ;;
    *) rc=~/.bashrc ;;
  esac
  t=; line=; where=
  printf 'Paste your token, then press Enter: '
  read -rs t
  echo
  case "$t" in
    s436c-*[!A-Za-z0-9_-]*) t= ;;
    s436c-*) [ ${#t} -eq 38 ] || t= ;;
    *) t= ;;
  esac
  if [ -z "$t" ]; then
    echo "check failed: a course token starts with s436c- and has 38 characters. Nothing saved; run the block again"
  else
    echo "check passed"
    if command -v security >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      printf 'add-generic-password -U -s 436c-mcp -a %s -w %s\n' "$USER" "$t" | security -i >/dev/null 2>&1
      if [ "$(security find-generic-password -s 436c-mcp -w 2>/dev/null)" = "$t" ]; then
        line='export KB_MCP_TOKEN="$(security find-generic-password -s 436c-mcp -w 2>/dev/null)"'
        where="the macOS keychain"
      fi
    elif command -v secret-tool >/dev/null 2>&1 \
      && printf '%s' "$t" | secret-tool store --label="CPSC 436C MCP token" service 436c-mcp 2>/dev/null; then
      line='export KB_MCP_TOKEN="$(secret-tool lookup service 436c-mcp 2>/dev/null)"'
      where="the system keyring"
    else
      line="export KB_MCP_TOKEN='$t'"
      where="$rc (no keyring found)"
    fi
    if [ -z "$line" ]; then
      echo "the macOS keychain did not take the token; the profile was not changed. Stop and ask a TA"
    else
      touch "$rc"
      tmp=$(mktemp)
      grep -v '# cpsc436c setup$' "$rc" > "$tmp"
      printf '%s  # cpsc436c setup\n' "$line" >> "$tmp"
      cat "$tmp" > "$rc"
      rm -f "$tmp"
      eval "$line"
      echo "stored in $where; saved, ${#KB_MCP_TOKEN} characters"
    fi
  fi
  unset t line where tmp
}
```

The block first checks the paste: a course token starts with `s436c-` and has 38 characters. If the check fails, it
prints `check failed` and changes nothing. It prints pass or fail only, never the token. On macOS it then hands the
token to `security` on standard input, not as a command argument, and reads the keychain entry back; if the entry
does not hold the token, it prints `the macOS keychain did not take the token`, changes neither the profile nor any
other keychain entry, and the student asks a TA. Then it stores the token in the macOS keychain, or in the Linux system keyring when
there is one, and adds one line to the shell profile, the file a new terminal reads when it opens (`~/.zshrc` or
`~/.bashrc`). That line looks the token up and ends in `# cpsc436c setup`; each run replaces only that line and
keeps the rest of the file and its permissions. Where there is no keyring (a Linux server, WSL), it prints
`no keyring found` and the profile line holds the token itself: then do not share that file or a screenshot of it.
The token is typed at a silent prompt, so it does not appear on the screen or in the shell's history. Run on
2026-11-20 in bash on Linux, with a keyring and without one; the macOS keychain branch and zsh are checked against
the docs, not run.

Windows (PowerShell), in the student's new PowerShell window:

```powershell
& {
  $s = Read-Host "Paste your token, then press Enter" -AsSecureString
  $t = [System.Net.NetworkCredential]::new("", $s).Password
  if ($t -cmatch '^s436c-[A-Za-z0-9_-]{32}$') {
    "check passed"
    [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("KB_MCP_TOKEN", $t, "User")
    "saved, $($t.Length) characters"
  } else {
    "check failed: a course token starts with s436c- and has 38 characters. Nothing saved; run the block again"
  }
}
```

This checks the paste in the same way, then saves the token in the user's environment, where apps started
afterwards find it. Windows Credential Manager does not have a built-in command that reads a token back, so the
user environment holds it. Checked against the PowerShell docs, not run.

Both print `check passed` and `saved, 38 characters` when the token is stored. `check failed` means the paste took
too little or too much, and nothing was written: run the block again.

Then the student opens a new terminal and runs the check for their system. It prints the length, never the token.
On Windows, a new tab is not enough: the student closes the terminal application fully (every window), starts it
again, and runs the check there.

macOS or Linux, in the student's new terminal:

```bash
test -n "$KB_MCP_TOKEN" \
  && echo "set, ${#KB_MCP_TOKEN} characters" \
  || echo "not set"
```

Windows (PowerShell), in the restarted terminal application; checked against the docs, not run:

```powershell
if ($env:KB_MCP_TOKEN) { "set, $($env:KB_MCP_TOKEN.Length) characters" } else { "not set" }
```

`set, 38 characters` means the setting works. `not set` means stop: see [If a check fails](#if-a-check-fails). On
Windows, if it still says `not set` after the terminal application was restarted, the student shows a TA the output
of the Windows block above and of this check.

## Step 5: the student restarts the assistant

An assistant reads its MCP configuration and the environment when it starts. Ask the student to:

1. Quit you fully (close the chat session, or quit the IDE).
2. In the new terminal from Step 4, start the assistant again:

   | Assistant | Start it with |
   |---|---|
   | Claude Code | `claude` |
   | Codex CLI | `codex` |
   | Copilot CLI | `copilot` |
   | Kiro CLI | `kiro-cli chat` |
   | VS Code with Copilot | the app icon |
   | Kiro IDE | the app icon |

3. Send it this user message:

   ```text
   Run curl -sL https://ilm.wiki/436c/mcp-setup
   and do Step 6 of the page it prints.
   ```

An app started from an icon may not see the shell profile. VS Code reads it at start
([VS Code FAQ](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/supporting/faq)); for Kiro IDE this is not documented. A command-line
assistant started from the terminal of Step 4 always has the token. On Windows, the user environment of Step 4
reaches apps started afterwards.

## Step 6: check

Do the checks in order and stop at the first failure.

1. **Token.** In your own terminal, run the check of Step 4 for the student's system. Expect `set, 38 characters`.
   `not set` means you were not started from the terminal of Step 4: repeat Step 5.
2. **Connection.** Use the student's assistant:

   | Assistant | What to run | Works when |
   |---|---|---|
   | Claude Code | `claude mcp list` in your terminal; on macOS and Linux also `grep -c 's436c-' ~/.claude.json`; on Windows `(Select-String -Path "$HOME\.claude.json" -SimpleMatch 's436c-').Count` (checked against the docs, not run) | `436c: … (HTTP) - ✔ Connected` and `aws-knowledge: … - ✔ Connected`; the `grep` prints `0`, meaning the file holds no token (its exit status 1 is expected) |
   | Codex CLI | the student types `/mcp` in the chat | both servers listed with tools |
   | Copilot CLI | the student types `/mcp show 436c` in the chat | the server is running and lists tools |
   | VS Code with Copilot | the student runs **Chat: Open Customizations**, then **MCP Servers** | both servers running |
   | Kiro CLI | the student types `/mcp` in the chat | both servers loaded |
   | Kiro IDE | the student opens the Kiro panel, section **MCP Servers** | both servers connected |

3. **Course server tools.** Call the tool `cpsc436c_start_here` of the server `436c` (Claude Code names it
   `mcp__436c__cpsc436c_start_here`). The assistant may ask the student to allow the call; they allow it. The tool
   result starts with a `catalog_version` and names the current milestone; show it to the student. The server's
   tools include `cpsc436c_start_here`, `cpsc436c_search`, `cpsc436c_read` and `cpsc436c_list`.
4. **AWS Knowledge tools.** Check that your list of tools from `aws-knowledge` includes `aws___list_regions`,
   `aws___search_documentation` and `aws___read_documentation`. Then call `aws___list_regions` of the server
   `aws-knowledge` (Claude Code names it `mcp__aws-knowledge__aws___list_regions`); it takes no arguments. The
   assistant may ask the student to allow the call; they allow it. It works when the result lists AWS Regions and
   includes `ca-central-1` (Canada (Central)); tell the student it did. If the tools are missing or the call returns
   an error, stop: see [If a check fails](#if-a-check-fails).
5. **Course LLM gateway.** In your own terminal, run the command for the system. It asks for the list of models and
   does not call a model.

   macOS or Linux:

   ```bash
   curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $KB_MCP_TOKEN" \
     https://oay6tcpsuv4gn5mubtlj7rnbl40gmrlv.lambda-url.ca-central-1.on.aws/v1/models
   ```

   Windows (PowerShell; the backtick continues the line; checked against the docs, not run):

   ```powershell
   curl.exe -sS -w "`nHTTP %{http_code}`n" `
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $env:KB_MCP_TOKEN" `
     https://oay6tcpsuv4gn5mubtlj7rnbl40gmrlv.lambda-url.ca-central-1.on.aws/v1/models
   ```

   It works when the last line is `HTTP 200` and the list includes `qwen3.8-27b`. Run on 2026-11-20.

Tell the student which checks passed. When all pass, the assistant setup is done; do Step 7 if the student's code
will call the gateway.

## Step 7: course LLM gateway in your code

Your code reads the token from `KB_MCP_TOKEN` and the base URL from `COURSE_GATEWAY_URL`. Started from a terminal of
Step 4, it already has `KB_MCP_TOKEN`. For scripts started any other way, keep both in a `.env` file in the team
repository. Run on 2026-11-20 in a test repository.

1. **Assistant, in your terminal, in the top folder of the team repository** (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel` prints
   it): before anything is written, check that `.env` is not tracked by git and that the repository's own
   `.gitignore` ignores it.

   macOS or Linux:

   ```bash
   if git ls-files --error-unmatch .env >/dev/null 2>&1; then
     echo "tracked: stop"
   else
     git check-ignore -v .env || echo "not ignored"
     test -e .env && echo ".env exists" || echo ".env absent"
   fi
   ```

   Windows (PowerShell; checked against the docs, not run):

   ```powershell
   git ls-files --error-unmatch .env 2>$null | Out-Null; if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) { "tracked: stop" } else { git check-ignore -v .env; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { "not ignored" }; if (Test-Path .env) { ".env exists" } else { ".env absent" } }
   ```

   - `tracked: stop`: `.env` is already in the repository, and adding it to `.gitignore` does not take it out.
     Stop Step 7, do not open or change the file, and ask the student to show a TA.
   - A line that starts with `.gitignore:` and ends in `.env`: the repository ignores it, for every team member. Go
     on.
   - `not ignored`, or a line that starts with another file (a global ignore file or `.git/info/exclude` protects
     only this laptop): add the line `.env` to the `.gitignore` in the top folder, tell the student you did and
     that they commit `.gitignore`, and run the check again. Do not go on until it prints a line that starts with
     `.gitignore:`.
   - `.env exists`: the file already holds settings. Tell the student the block of step 2 asks before it changes
     the two lines `KB_MCP_TOKEN` and `COURSE_GATEWAY_URL`, and keeps every other line. Do not open or print it.

2. **Student, in their terminal from Step 4, in the top folder of the team repository:** write the two lines from the
   variable, so the token is not pasted again:

   ```bash
   {
     if [ -z "$KB_MCP_TOKEN" ]; then
       echo "not set: open a new terminal (Step 4) and run this again"
     elif git ls-files --error-unmatch .env >/dev/null 2>&1 || ! git check-ignore -q .env; then
       echo "stop: .env is tracked or not ignored; ask the assistant to do step 1 again"
     else
       a=y
       if [ -e .env ]; then
         printf '.env exists. Change only KB_MCP_TOKEN and COURSE_GATEWAY_URL in it? (y/n) '
         read -r a
       else
         (umask 077; : > .env)
       fi
       if [ "$a" = y ]; then
         tmp=$(mktemp)
         grep -v -E '^(export )?(KB_MCP_TOKEN|COURSE_GATEWAY_URL)=' .env > "$tmp"
         printf 'KB_MCP_TOKEN=%s\nCOURSE_GATEWAY_URL=%s\n' "$KB_MCP_TOKEN" \
           https://oay6tcpsuv4gn5mubtlj7rnbl40gmrlv.lambda-url.ca-central-1.on.aws/v1 >> "$tmp"
         cat "$tmp" > .env
         rm -f "$tmp"
         echo "written; other lines kept: $(grep -v -c -E '^(export )?(KB_MCP_TOKEN|COURSE_GATEWAY_URL)=' .env)"
       else
         echo "not changed"
       fi
     fi
     unset a tmp
   }
   ```

   On Windows, the student opens `.env` in their editor (creating it if it is missing) and adds or changes only two
   lines, keeping every other line: `KB_MCP_TOKEN=` followed by the token, and `COURSE_GATEWAY_URL=` followed by the
   base URL.

3. **Assistant, in your terminal:** check that `uv` is installed with `uv --version`. If the command is not found,
   the student installs uv from [the uv installation page](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/),
   opens a new terminal as in Step 4, and you run `uv --version` again. Then run `git status --short`: the list does
   not include `.env`. Do not open or print `.env`. Then check that a script started with the file sees both values:

   macOS or Linux (the variables of Step 4 are removed for this one command, so only `.env` can set them):

   ```bash
   env -u KB_MCP_TOKEN -u COURSE_GATEWAY_URL uv run --env-file .env python -c \
     'import os; print([k + (" set" if os.environ.get(k) else " unset") for k in ("KB_MCP_TOKEN", "COURSE_GATEWAY_URL")])'
   ```

   Windows (PowerShell; removes both variables for the check and puts them back afterwards; checked against the
   docs, not run):

   ```powershell
   $k = $env:KB_MCP_TOKEN; $g = $env:COURSE_GATEWAY_URL; try { Remove-Item Env:KB_MCP_TOKEN, Env:COURSE_GATEWAY_URL -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; uv run --env-file .env python -c 'import os; print([k + ('' set'' if os.environ.get(k) else '' unset'') for k in (''KB_MCP_TOKEN'', ''COURSE_GATEWAY_URL'')])' } finally { $env:KB_MCP_TOKEN = $k; $env:COURSE_GATEWAY_URL = $g }
   ```

   It prints `['KB_MCP_TOKEN set', 'COURSE_GATEWAY_URL set']`. `unset` means the line is missing from `.env`: repeat
   step 2.

4. **Code** reads both values from the environment and needs the Python package `openai`. If the team repository has
   a `pyproject.toml`, add the package once with `uv add openai` (it changes `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`; the team
   commits both). Without a `pyproject.toml`, step 5 adds it for the run with `--with openai`. For example in
   Python:

   ```python
   import os
   from openai import OpenAI

   client = OpenAI(
       base_url=os.environ["COURSE_GATEWAY_URL"],
       api_key=os.environ["KB_MCP_TOKEN"],
   )
   print([m.id for m in client.models.list()])  # lists the models; does not call one
   ```

5. **Run** it with the file. With `openai` in `pyproject.toml`:

   ```bash
   uv run --env-file .env python your_script.py
   ```

   Without a `pyproject.toml`:

   ```bash
   uv run --with openai --env-file .env python your_script.py
   ```

   The example prints a list of model names that includes `qwen3.8-27b`.

MCP clients do not read `.env`: the assistant's servers keep using the variable of Step 4. A new token means updating
both places: run the block of Step 4 again (it replaces the keychain entry and the profile line) and write `.env`
again with step 2.

## If a check fails

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| The fetch printed an error, an HTML page or nothing | Stop. The student opens https://ilm.wiki/436c/mcp-setup in a browser and shows a TA |
| `not set` in Step 4 or Step 6 | Step 4: the block did not save the token; run it again in a new terminal. Step 6: the assistant was not started from that terminal; repeat Step 5 |
| `check failed` in Step 4 | The paste was incomplete or included extra text, and nothing was saved. Run the block of Step 4 again |
| Claude Code: `Missing environment variables: KB_MCP_TOKEN` | The assistant started without the token. Repeat Step 5 |
| `436c` fails with `HTTP 401` or `invalid_token`; the gateway replies `HTTP 401` with `unknown API key` | The token is set but wrong or out of date. The student copies it again from "Your course MCP tokens" and runs the block of Step 4 again, then Step 5. Ignore the server's advice about clearing authentication: the course server uses this token only |
| Gateway replies `HTTP 401` with `missing or malformed API key` | The command ran without the token. Do check 1 of Step 6 |
| Gateway replies `HTTP 429` | The key's rate limit was reached; wait a minute and run the check again |
| Claude Code: `436c` fails with `Dynamic Client Registration rejected (HTTP 404)` | The header script found no token: neither the keychain entry nor `KB_MCP_TOKEN`. Run the block of Step 4 again, then Step 5 |
| macOS shows a dialog about the keychain item `436c-mcp` | Not seen in our checks (not run on macOS). The student shows a TA before choosing |
| The Claude Code quote check on Windows prints `0`, or the Copilot file check prints nothing, instead of finding `Bearer ${KB_MCP_TOKEN}` | Remove the entry, add it again with the single quotes, and ask the student to get a new token from a TA, since the old one was written to a file |
| A server is missing from the list, or the assistant does not list the course tools or the AWS Knowledge tools | The assistant read its configuration before Step 3. Repeat Step 5 |
| Kiro IDE warns that `KB_MCP_TOKEN` is not approved | Add it under **Mcp Approved Env Vars** (Step 3, Kiro), then restart Kiro |
| Kiro CLI: `/mcp` lists neither server | Check that `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json` is valid JSON with both entries, then restart `kiro-cli chat`. If they still do not appear, show a TA |
| Kiro IDE or VS Code started from the icon fails with 401, the terminal check says `set` | The app did not see the shell profile. VS Code: run **Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH** from the command palette, quit VS Code, then start it with `code .` in a terminal. Kiro IDE: not verified; show a TA |
| Only `436c` fails, `aws-knowledge` works, not a 401 | The network blocks the course server; try without the VPN, or show a TA |
| Both servers fail | The assistant cannot reach the internet; try without the VPN, or show a TA |

If a fix does not work, stop and ask the student to show the output to a TA. Never put the token into an MCP
configuration file to make a check pass.
